texts.facts: 1. This order shall decide an appeal filed under Section 70 of Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 (hereinafter referred to "FSS Act") assailing the impugned order dated 02.06.2021 passed by the Ld. Adjudicating Officer (ADM), District East, Delhi in the case title Food Safety Officer v. Shiv Kumar Goel & Others, imposing a penalty of Rs.10,000/ each upon appellant nos.1,2&3 and Rs.20,000/ each upon appellant nos. 4,5&6 under Section 52 of FSS Act. 2. The facts giving rise to the present case are that the sample of "Bhujia" were taken by the Food Safety Officer (hereinafter referred to 'FSO'), which consisted of four sealed packets of 400 grams, having identical label & declaration for analysis on 11.10.2018 from M/s Aggarwal Super Store situated at C19/54, Nehru Market, Kalyanpuri, Delhi91, which is the proprietorship concern of appellant no.2 and was being marketed by appellant Shiv Kumar Goel (appellant no.1). A fortiori there are no question raised as about the procedural compliance committed by the FSO and suffice to state that one counterpart of the sample was sent to Food Analyst, Government of Delhi laboratory situated at Lawrence Road, Industrial Area, Delhi, which after analysis vide report dated 25.10.2018 brought out that the sample was "misbranded" on account of violation of Rules 2.2.2.2(c), 2.2.2.5(ii)(b) and 2.2.2.10 of the Food Safety & Standards (Packaging & Labelling) Regulation, 2011 (hereinafter referred to "FSSPL Regulation, 2011"), since the name of the specific 'edible oil' was not declared in the list of ingredients besides not mentioning or declaring the type of flavouring agent as per Regulation 2.2.2.5(ii)(b) of FSSPL Regulation, 2011; and as also holding that the "best before date" was not declared as per Regulation 2.2.2.10 of FSSPL Regulation, 2011. Accordingly, the Ld. Adjudicating Officer after holding inquiry imposed the aforementioned fine/penalty in terms of Section 52 of the FSS Act. 3. On filing of the present appeal, the operation of the impugned order was stayed by the Ld. Predecessor of this court (as his lordship was then) vide order dated 23.07.2021 subject to furnishing of the DD/FDR/Bank Guarantee for the amount equivalent to the penalty/fine imposed by the Ld. Adjudicating Officer, which was complied with. 4. Notice has been issued to the respondent/State and a reply has been filed, to which a rejoinder was also filed and the narratives of the same are not mentioned for the sake of brevity since the present appeal pertains to only raising of a legal issue with no denial on factual aspects. In short, the appellants have assailed the impugned order primarily on the grounds that the Delhi Laboratory was not competent as per Section 43 of FSS Act; and that the Adjudicating Officer failed to appreciate the order dated 17.07.2018, followed by another clarification dated 17.01.2020 and Section 16(5) of FSS Act enjoins upon the Food Authority to issue "improvement notices" for such minor labeling violations instead of launching reckless prosecution; and lastly that Adjudicating Authority failed to appreciate that sampled commodity i.e. Bhujia was manufactured by respondent nos. 4,5&6 and was supplied to them against valid invoices and therefore, the Adjudicating Authority should have accorded benefit to the appellants in terms of Section 80(B)(2)(a) of FSS Act.
texts.arguments: Counsel for the appellant has relied upon the decision in R. Chandershekhran & Anr. v. State of Madras 2017(1) FAC 88 and M/s Nestle India Ltd v. Food Safety and Standards Authority of India and Ors. 2015(2) FAC 56. Further, Section 16(1) of the FSS Act enumerates the duties and function of the Food Authority to regulate and monitor the manufacture, processing, distribution, sale and import of food as to ensure safe and wholesome food and Section 16(5) of the FSS Act stipulates that directions given by the Food Authority from time to time on matters relating to food safety and standards shall be binding upon the Commissioner of Food Safety. Section 80 of the FSS Act provides for defences that may or may not be allowed in prosecution/adjudication under this Act and vide subsection (B) of Section 80 FSS Act, the defence of due diligence is allowed to the effect of the defaulter proving taking of all reasonable precautions and exercise of due diligence to prevent the commission of the offence under the Act that is alleged to have been committed by that person or by another person under his control. Reverting to the instant matter, First thing first, there is considerable merit in the plea taken by Ld. Counsel for the appellants that the sampled item was tested at Delhi Lab that was submitted on Shiv Kumar Goel Ors. vs . Fso Page 1 Of 12 on 23 July, 2022 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/199824274/ 3 12.10.2018 and then the report was made available on 25.10.2018 but the Laboratory was not a recognized and accredited as on that day in terms of Section 43 of the FSS Act since the notification for approving the laboratory was issued by the Government of NCT of Delhi on 13.02.2020. In this regard, reference can be made to the cited case titled "Nestle India Ltd. Vs. The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India" (supra), wherein it was also held that it was incumbent in adjudication/prosecution under FSS Act that not only the food analyst but also the laboratory itself should be recognized and accredited by the Food Authority and since on that day when the samples were tested, the laboratory was not recognized and there was no accreditation to the competency of the food analyst under Section 45 of the FSS Act, and it was held that the said report cannot be relied upon.
